content:
The international research team has made significant progress in understanding the behavior of black hole jets, powerful streams of matter that can extend far beyond the objects that produce them.

These jets are believed to play an important role in shaping galaxies and regulating their evolution. Yet scientists have long struggled to determine precisely how much energy they carry and how that energy affects the surrounding environment.

The new study provides valuable measurements that could help address these questions, offering fresh insight into some of the most extreme physical processes in the universe.

Observations of Cygnus X-1

Using an Earth-sized virtual radio telescope, the researchers observed jets of matter emerging from Cygnus X-1, a binary star system containing the first black hole whose existence was confirmed.

The observations provide new information about how these powerful outflows behave and how they interact with the material surrounding the black hole.

Such interactions are particularly important because black hole jets can influence the formation and evolution of galaxies, redistributing energy into their environments.

To investigate the phenomenon, scientists combined observations from a network of radio telescopes using a technique known as interferometry.

By linking multiple instruments, they effectively created a single virtual telescope with an observing capability comparable to that of a telescope the size of Earth.

This approach allowed the team to examine changes in the jets over time and reconstruct their movements in remarkable detail.

The observations revealed that the jets were being deflected by powerful stellar winds as the black hole moved along its orbit.

The researchers compared this behavior to the way strong winds on Earth can push and distort the stream of water emerging from a fountain.

By measuring how far the jets were bent by these stellar winds, the team was able to calculate their instantaneous power for the first time.

The results were remarkable.

The researchers determined that the jets carried power equivalent to approximately 10,000 Suns, demonstrating the enormous amount of energy involved and the potential influence of these outflows on their cosmic surroundings.

They also measured the speed of the material traveling through the jets.

According to the study, the jets move at approximately 150,000 kilometers per second (93,200 miles per second), equivalent to roughly half the speed of light.

These measurements provide important new constraints on the physical processes taking place around black holes, where matter experiences extreme gravitational forces before some of it is expelled in powerful jets.

Another particularly significant finding concerns the amount of energy transferred into these outflows.

The researchers concluded that approximately 10% of the energy released by matter falling toward the black hole is carried away by the jets.

Although theoretical models had previously suggested such a relationship, directly verifying it through observations had proved difficult.

The new measurements therefore provide valuable evidence supporting existing theories and establish a stronger foundation for future investigations.

Implications for theoretical physics and cosmology

The study was conducted by researchers from the Curtin Institute of Radio Astronomy (CIRA) and the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), in collaboration with the University of Oxford.

The findings were published in the scientific journal Nature Astronomy.

Dr. Steve Prabu, the study’s lead author, explained that a sequence of images showing the jets’ changing positions was essential to obtaining the new measurements.

He described the phenomenon as “dancing jets,” referring to the way the outflows appeared to move as stellar winds pushed them away from their original paths.

By following these movements, the researchers were able to estimate how much energy the jets carry and how that energy is transferred into the surrounding environment.

According to Prabu, this information is essential for understanding what proportion of the energy released near a black hole ultimately influences the material around Cygnus X-1.

The findings therefore extend beyond the behavior of a single binary system.

They could help scientists better understand the relationship between black holes and the environments in which they exist, including the ways energetic jets can affect the structure and evolution of galaxies.

These discoveries could open new avenues for investigating black hole behavior and understanding the role these objects play throughout the universe.

The ability to measure changes in jet behavior over time represents an important advance for astrophysical research.

It allows scientists to investigate how black holes transfer energy into their surroundings rather than relying exclusively on theoretical estimates.

This is particularly valuable because black holes can influence matter across enormous distances, making their energetic activity an important factor in models of galactic development.

The new observations could also help researchers refine their understanding of the physical conditions that produce powerful jets and determine how efficiently energy is transported away from the material surrounding a black hole.

More broadly, the study provides additional evidence that can be used to test and improve theoretical descriptions of black hole activity.

Such measurements are essential for advancing astrophysics, where understanding the behavior of matter and energy under extreme conditions remains a major scientific challenge.

By confirming important predictions and providing previously unavailable observational data, the research strengthens the connection between theoretical physics and the actual behavior of black holes.

It also offers scientists new opportunities to explore how these objects contribute to the large-scale evolution of the universe.

Ultimately, the observations of Cygnus X-1 represent an important step toward understanding how black holes release, transport, and redistribute energy.

The results not only support existing theoretical models but also provide new information that could guide future research in astrophysics and help refine our understanding of the energetic processes that shape galaxies and the wider cosmos.
